transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I came in today because... I've started to feel, in a quiet but pretty stubborn way, that the best version of my life is just behind me. It's... it feels like no amount of planning or discipline on my part is going to get me back to feeling like myself.
How long have you been feeling this way — that your best days are behind you and that things won't improve?

It's been a while. This has really been going on since... well, since a hiking injury I had a little over three years ago. I'd say it's been about three years and three months now, if I had to put an exact timeline on it.

Over these past three years, have there been stretches of time — maybe weeks or months — where your mood felt noticeably better, or has this feeling of hopelessness and that your best days are behind you been present pretty much the entire time?

Not really, no. I mean, maybe there's a day here or there where I'm just a bit more distracted, but... as far as actual weeks or months where I felt noticeably better? I haven't had anything like that. It's pretty much just been this steady, flat feeling the entire time.
Before the hiking injury three years ago, how would you describe your typical mood? Were you generally feeling well and able to enjoy things?

Before the injury? I was... well, I was fine. I felt normal. I enjoyed things, yeah. I retired a bit early, and I was spending a lot of time outdoors, staying active. My mood was good. I didn't have this... heavy feeling hanging over me back then. I was just living my life.

Have you ever had periods, even brief ones, where your mood was unusually high or energetic — where you felt more optimistic, needed less sleep, or had racing thoughts — rather than just the flat, heavy feeling you've described?

No, I haven't had anything like that. I've never felt unusually high or energetic. I've always just needed my regular amount of sleep, and my thoughts don't race. It's just been this same low, flat feeling since the injury.

During these three years since the hiking injury, have there been any weeks or even just a few days in a row where you felt even slightly less heavy or flat — maybe where you had a bit more energy or found something mildly enjoyable — or has it truly been unrelenting without any breaks at all?

No, not really. Like I said, there hasn't been any break. It's just been... unrelenting, I guess is the word you used. I haven't had any days or weeks where I felt lighter or had more energy. It's just been the same flat feeling the whole time.

Over these past three years, have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy — like the outdoor activities and hiking you mentioned — or do you still want to do those things but just can't seem to get yourself to do them?

I haven't really lost interest, exactly. I still think about hiking and being outdoors... I want to do those things. But I just don't have the drive to actually go do them anymore. I just can't seem to get myself out the door.
When you say the flat feeling has been unrelenting, do you mean there hasn't been a single day in these three years where your mood lifted at all, even for just a few hours?
I mean, maybe for an hour or two here and there if a friend calls or something, but... no, not really. It never lasts. The heavy feeling is always right there waiting. It's just a constant weight.

I want to make sure I haven't missed anything — have you ever had a period, even a short one, where you felt unusually confident, more talkative than usual, or like you could take on a lot of projects at once?
No, I've never felt like that. I've never had any times where I felt overly confident or talkative, or like I had all this energy to do things. It's just been the opposite, really.
Since the hiking injury, have there ever been times when you needed significantly less sleep than usual — say, feeling rested after only 3 or 4 hours — without feeling exhausted during the day?

No, never anything like that. I've never been the kind of person who could just run on three or four hours of sleep and feel fine. If I don't get a full night's rest, I definitely feel it the next day. So, no, I haven't had any periods where I felt rested on less sleep.
Have you ever had a period where you felt exceptionally creative, had lots of new ideas, or started multiple projects that you wouldn't normally take on — even if it only lasted a few days?

No, I can't say I have. I've never really had a burst of creativity or anything like that where I'm starting a bunch of new things. Honestly, it's a struggle just to keep up with the normal day-to-day stuff, let alone taking on extra projects. So, no, nothing like that.
Have you ever had a period — even just a few days — where you felt noticeably more irritable or impatient than your usual baseline, even if you didn't feel energetic or happy?

No, not really. I mean, I get frustrated sometimes like anyone else, but I haven't had any stretch of days where I was just unusually irritable or snapping at people. My mood is pretty flat most of the time, so... no, I haven't noticed anything like that.

I want to go back to something — in those three years since the injury, has there ever been a time, even just a few days, where you felt more talkative than usual, or where you were more focused on getting things done, even if you didn't necessarily feel happy or energetic?

No, I haven't. I'm not a very talkative person to begin with, and I definitely haven't had any days where I was suddenly chatting more or laser-focused on getting things done. Like I said, it's mostly just been a low, flat feeling for a long time now. I just kind of get through the day.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent, unrelenting depressed mood lasting over 3 years since a clear precipitating event (hiking injury). Key features include: chronic depressed mood described as 'flat' and 'heavy,' anhedonia (loss of drive for previously enjoyed activities), absence of any manic or hypomanic episodes despite explicit screening, minimal day-to-day mood variation, and clear functional impairment. The chronicity (>3 years), stability of symptoms without significant remission periods, and absence of bipolar features are consistent with Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia). While F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode) and F43.21 (Adjustment Disorder with depressed mood) were considered, the 3+ year duration without substantial recovery and the patient's description of a 'steady, flat feeling the entire time' best fit the diagnostic criteria for F34.1.
